question: Compare the evaluation design of LiveCodeBench and Bench-Push. For each benchmark, state what is being evaluated, what makes the test setting realistic or reproducible, and what metrics or task categories are used.

## LiveCodeBench
- **What is being evaluated:** LiveCodeBench evaluates “LLMs for code” and “code capabilities,” with scenarios including **code generation**, **self-repair**, and **code execution**. It also emphasizes “broader coding abilities” beyond natural language-to-code tasks. [Source 1] [Source 3] [Source 9]
- **What makes the setting realistic or reproducible:**  
  - It is **contamination-free / live**: problems have **release dates**, enabling evaluation over different time windows and helping detect or avoid contamination. [Source 6]  
  - Problems are sourced from **reputable competition websites**—LeetCode, AtCoder, and CodeForces—where problems are already vetted by platform users, and they come with hidden tests. [Source 1] [Source 11]  
  - The benchmark uses a **good number of tests** per problem, “about 17 on average,” to support robust evaluation while still finishing quickly. [Source 1]  
  - For code execution, it uses a pool of **correct, human-submitted solutions** with compile-time and runtime filtering plus manual inspection. [Source 3]
- **Metrics or task categories used:**  
  - Task categories/scenarios include **code generation**, **self-repair**, and **code execution**. [Source 3]  
  - The context does **not provide the exact metric name(s)** for LiveCodeBench in the retrieved passages; it only says the collected/generated tests are used to evaluate correctness. [Source 3]

## Bench-Push
- **What is being evaluated:** Bench-Push evaluates **policies** for mobile robot pushing tasks. The tasks are of two types: **navigation tasks** and **manipulation tasks**. [Source 4]
- **What makes the setting realistic or reproducible:**  
  - It provides **high-fidelity 3D simulations** with MuJoCo to enable physical robot deployment, plus **2D Pymunk simulations** for rapid prototyping. [Source 5]  
  - The benchmark is designed for **sim-to-real transfer**, and results on the physical testbed generally align with simulation. [Source 5] [Source 8]  
  - It offers **customizable tasks** with varying complexity. [Source 8]
- **Metrics or task categories used:**  
  - Task categories are explicitly **navigation** and **manipulation**. [Source 4]  
  - The benchmark introduces **novel metrics** that capture **efficiency**, **interaction trade-offs**, and **partial task completions**; it also uses separate metrics for pushing-based navigation and manipulation tasks. [Source 5] [Source 7]  
  - The context does **not give the exact metric formulas or names** in the retrieved passages. [Source 7] [Source 4]

## Bottom line
- **LiveCodeBench** is a benchmark for **code-capability evaluation** with **live, contamination-aware, competition-sourced problems** and multiple scenario types. [Source 6] [Source 11]  
- **Bench-Push** is a benchmark for **robot pushing policies** with **simulation and physical-testbed realism**, focused on **navigation/manipulation** tasks and **efficiency/interaction-oriented metrics**. [Source 5] [Source 7]

Evaluation metrics in existing mobile robot bench-

8
Conclusion
In this work, we propose LiveCodeBench, a new benchmark for evaluating LLMs for code. Our
benchmark mitigates contamination issues in existing benchmarks by introducing live evaluations
and emphasizing scenarios beyond code generation to account for the broader coding abilities of
LLMs. LiveCodeBench is an extensible framework, that will keep on updating with new problems,
scenarios, and models. Our evaluations reveal novel findings such as contamination detection and
potential overfitting on HumanEval. We hope LiveCodeBench with serve to advance understand-
ing of current code LLMs and also guide future research in this area through our findings.

3
Benchmark Curation
We curate our problems from three coding competition websites: LeetCode, AtCoder, and Code-
Forces. These websites periodically host contests containing problems that assess the coding and
problem-solving skills of participants. The problems consist of a natural language problem state-
ment along with example input-output examples, and the goal is to write a program that passes
a set of hidden tests. Further, thousands of participants participate, solving these problems thus
ensuring that the problems are vetted for clarity and correctness.
